newsitem.title: USA: U.S. blacks entering hospital may be less ill - study.
newsitem.headline: U.S. blacks entering hospital may be less ill - study.

text.p: Black patients admitted to hospitals were not as ill as white patients and were less likely to die, according to a study released Tuesday.

A study by Case Western Reserve University researchers in Cleveland found the risk of death among black in-patients was 20 percent lower than among whites and the black patients were more likely to be younger and female.

The black patients were also more likely to have been admitted from emergency rooms and to lack medical insurance, wrote Howard Gordon, now at Baylor College of Medicine in Houston, in the Journal of the American Medical Association.

The study examined more than 88,000 patients, of whom 22 percent were black, in northeastern Ohio who were suffering from commonly treated medical conditions such as heart problems, obstructed airways, gastrointestinal hemorrhages, pneumonia and strokes.

Because blacks admitted to hospitals were less likely to have a primary care physician and were in danger of missing out on regular follow-up care, they were more likely to receive costly in-patient treatment, Gordon wrote.
